10-Week ML/AI Internship Prep: Plan Evaluation & Complete
Roadmap
TL;DR
Your original study guide is a solid 7.5/10 — well-structured and covers the right topics, but it critically
misses Data Structures & Algorithms (DSA) and underestimates the time needed for hands-on
projects. For an ML/AI internship, DSA isn’t just “nice to have” — it’s the gatekeeper to getting past
technical interviews. With 40 hours/week over 10 weeks, this enhanced plan adds DSA alongside your

technical interviews. With 40 hours/week over 10 weeks, this enhanced plan adds DSA alongside your
original roadmap, integrates the best free resources for each topic, and allocates 20+ hours in the final
weeks exclusively to portfolio projects. The result: a rigorous, interview-ready preparation that
transforms your guide from a learning curriculum into a job-winning system.
1. Rating Your Original Plan: Strengths & Gaps

1. Rating Your Original Plan: Strengths & Gaps
Your original study guide demonstrates excellent strategic thinking about ML/AI skill acquisition. The
phased approach — moving from Python foundations through data literacy, hands-on AI models, core
ML, LLMs, and finally real-world projects — follows a pedagogically sound progression. As someone
with a CE background transitioning to MSCS, you’re in an ideal position to execute this because you

with a CE background transitioning to MSCS, you’re in an ideal position to execute this because you
already understand programming fundamentals, computer architecture, and likely have some exposure
to algorithms. This isn’t starting from zero; it’s redirecting existing engineering instincts toward ML/
AI-specific tooling and workflows.
The plan’s most significant strength is its emphasis on project-based learning. Too many ML learners

get stuck in “tutorial hell” — consuming courses without ever building anything original. Your Step 6
(“Build Lots of Real-World AI Applications”) and the inclusion of mini-project workflows within each
step show you understand that portfolios get interviews, not certificates. The coverage of modern
AI tooling — LangChain, RAG, vector databases, Streamlit — is particularly strong and aligned with
what ML engineering teams actually use in 2025 (wordpress.com) . The recognition that no-code/low-

what ML engineering teams actually use in 2025 (wordpress.com) . The recognition that no-code/low-
code tools (Crew AI, Langflow, n8n) have a place in an engineer’s toolkit also shows practical maturity
— knowing when to reach for a visual workflow builder versus writing Python from scratch is a genuinely
valuable skill.
However, there are three critical gaps that would prevent this plan from reliably landing an ML/AI

However, there are three critical gaps that would prevent this plan from reliably landing an ML/AI
internship. First and most importantly: the complete absence of Data Structures & Algorithms
(DSA). Technical interviews for ML/AI roles still test coding problem-solving — not at FAANG-hard
levels necessarily, but you’ll absolutely face LeetCode-style questions. LogicMojo’s analysis of 200+ suc-
cessful AI placements found that candidates who practiced DSA alongside ML learning had significantly

higher success rates (logicmojo) . Second, the original plan lacks specific resource recommendations be-
yond generic library names — “learn pandas” is good direction, but without knowing whether to use
Kaggle Learn, DataCamp, or a YouTube playlist, a beginner wastes hours evaluating options instead of
learning. Third, the timeline is too compressed for genuine competency — 10 weeks is achievable, but

only with extremely focused resource selection and aggressive project milestones. Without these addi-
tions, the plan risks producing a learner who can discuss ML concepts but struggles to pass a coding
screen or demonstrate production-ready skills.

2. Why DSA Is Non-Negotiable for ML/AI Internships
The ML/AI field has a peculiar dual gatekeeping system. On one side, you need ML competency —
knowing how to clean data, train models, evaluate performance, and deploy solutions. On the other

knowing how to clean data, train models, evaluate performance, and deploy solutions. On the other
side, you need software engineering fundamentals — and DSA is the universal language of technical
interviewing. Even ML research internships at top companies include coding assessments. The NeetCode
150/250 curriculum, built by a former Google SWE, has become the de facto standard for structured
DSA preparation because it organizes problems by topic with dependency-aware sequencing (PracHub)

DSA preparation because it organizes problems by topic with dependency-aware sequencing (PracHub)
. Following this alongside your ML learning ensures you don’t become the candidate who can explain
transformer architectures but can’t invert a binary tree.
The good news is that DSA for ML roles is less intense than for pure SWE roles.
You’re
not grinding LeetCode Hard graph problems daily. Most ML/AI internship interviews focus on Arrays,

not grinding LeetCode Hard graph problems daily. Most ML/AI internship interviews focus on Arrays,
HashMaps, Two Pointers, Sliding Window, basic Trees, and simple Dynamic Programming — roughly
the first half of NeetCode 150 (logicmojo) . The recommended approach in this plan dedicates 8-12
hours per week consistently to DSA practice, which is suﬀicient to build interview-ready competency
without derailing your ML learning. This parallel-track approach mirrors what successful candidates

without derailing your ML learning. This parallel-track approach mirrors what successful candidates
actually do — LogicMojo’s mentorship data shows that students who ran DSA practice alongside AI
learning (rather than sequencing them) had measurably better placement outcomes (logicmojo) .
DSA practice also has a surprising secondary benefit for ML work: it sharpens the exact type of
structured thinking that debugging ML pipelines requires. When you’re tracking down why your

structured thinking that debugging ML pipelines requires. When you’re tracking down why your
neural network’s loss isn’t converging, the systematic debugging approach you developed solving LeetCode
problems transfers directly. The pattern-matching skills from recognizing that a problem is a “sliding
window” variant mirror the intuition for recognizing that a dataset needs a particular preprocessing

approach. DSA isn’t interview trivia — it’s deliberate practice for the problem-solving loops you’ll run
constantly as an ML engineer.

The schedule below allocates 40 hours per week across six focus areas: Python (CS50P), DSA (Neet-
Code/LeetCode), SQL & Data Literacy, ML Fundamentals (scikit-learn/PyTorch), AI/LLMs & Agents
(LangChain/RAG), and Projects & Portfolio. The allocation shifts progressively from foundations (Weeks
1-3) through ML core (Weeks 4-6) and AI/LLMs (Weeks 7-8) to an intensive project sprint (Weeks 9-10).

Week 1 front-loads Python because your CE background means you can accelerate through CS50P faster
than a complete beginner.
CS50P is the best Python foundation course available — it’s taught by
David Malan with Harvard-level rigor, covers not just syntax but code style, type hints, docstrings, list
comprehensions, and generators that most beginner courses skip (rivenintech.com) . The problem sets

comprehensions, and generators that most beginner courses skip (rivenintech.com) . The problem sets
are genuinely engaging and build real skills. Don’t skip the “Et Cetera” lecture — it covers Pythonic
patterns you’ll use constantly.
DSA starts immediately with NeetCode’s Arrays & Hashing section because these are the most fre-
quently asked problem types and they require minimal algorithmic theory to get started. The pattern of

“use a HashMap for O(1) lookups” is something you’ll internalize quickly and use constantly. Aim for 5
problems in the first week — quality over quantity, with full understanding of the optimal solution.
SQLBolt is the fastest path to SQL fundamentals — it’s entirely browser-based, requires no setup, and
covers 90% of the SQL you’ll write in real-world data work (ai2sql.io) . Lessons 1-9 take you from basic

SELECT queries through JOINs and NULL handling. The interactive exercises give immediate feedback,
which is crucial for early SQL learning where syntax errors are frustratingly opaque.

Week 3 is the data literacy consolidation week. Pandas merging, multi-indexing, and time-series
handling are the operations you’ll perform in virtually every ML project.
The Kaggle Learn micro-
courses combined with the oﬀicial pandas documentation provide both guided learning and reference

courses combined with the oﬀicial pandas documentation provide both guided learning and reference
material. For visualization, seaborn’s statistical plotting capabilities (distribution plots, regression plots,
categorical plots) produce publication-quality figures with minimal code — understanding when to use
each plot type is a skill that distinguishes competent data scientists from beginners (KDnuggets) .

each plot type is a skill that distinguishes competent data scientists from beginners (KDnuggets) .
The EDA (Exploratory Data Analysis) project is your first mini-portfolio piece. Pick a Kaggle dataset
with interesting features — the Titanic dataset is classic for beginners, or choose something domain-
relevant to your interests. The goal isn’t model building yet; it’s demonstrating that you can load data,

handle missing values, create informative visualizations, and extract actionable insights. This project
goes on your GitHub with a clean README.
DSA progresses to Binary Search and Sliding Window — both are high-frequency interview patterns.
Binary Search variants (finding boundaries, rotated arrays) appear constantly because they’re easy to
explain but have subtle edge cases that trip up unprepared candidates. Sliding Window is essential for

substring/subarray problems and has direct analogies to batch processing in ML pipelines.

Week 4 introduces the Andrew Ng Machine Learning Specialization — the single most recom-
mended ML course for beginners, with over 5 million enrolled students (wordpress.com) . The specializa-
tion’s strength is diagnostic vocabulary: understanding why models underfit, overfit, or fail to generalize.

This conceptual foundation prevents the common beginner mistake of throwing neural networks at every
problem without understanding whether the issue is data quality, feature engineering, or model selection.
The course uses Python, NumPy, and scikit-learn — tools you’re already familiar with from Weeks 1-3.
Parallel to the course, start reading Aurélien Géron’s “Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-
Learn, Keras & TensorFlow” — widely considered the best practical ML book (FreeCodecamp) .

Learn, Keras & TensorFlow” — widely considered the best practical ML book (FreeCodecamp) .
The book’s Chapter 2 presents a complete end-to-end ML project (predicting California housing prices)
that demonstrates the full workflow: data exploration, preprocessing, model selection, cross-validation,
hyperparameter tuning, and deployment. Working through this alongside Andrew Ng’s theory creates a

hyperparameter tuning, and deployment. Working through this alongside Andrew Ng’s theory creates a
powerful learn-by-doing loop. Géron’s book is particularly valuable because it’s written by a practitioner
(former YouTube video classification lead) and includes production-ready techniques that courses often
skip (ML in Production) .
scikit-learn is the primary library for classical ML — it implements virtually every algorithm you’ll need

with a consistent API: fit(), predict(), score() (Wikitechy) . By Week 4, you should be comfortable
with the standard workflow: train_test_split →preprocessing pipeline →model fitting →evaluation
metrics. Implementing Linear Regression and Logistic Regression from scratch (using NumPy) alongside
scikit-learn’s built-in versions deepens understanding of what the library is actually doing under the hood.

Week 5 expands your algorithm toolkit while starting your first significant ML project: a Customer
Churn Predictor. This is a classic binary classification problem that demonstrates end-to-end ML
competency — data collection (use a public telecom dataset), cleaning, feature engineering, model training
(compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost), evaluation (precision, recall, F1-score —

not just accuracy), and a simple Streamlit dashboard for predictions. The project should be GitHub-ready
with a comprehensive README explaining your methodology and results.
Feature engineering is where ML transitions from “running library functions” to “genuine data science
intuition”. Understanding when to create interaction terms, how to handle categorical variables (one-hot
encoding vs. target encoding), and why feature scaling matters for some algorithms but not others —

encoding vs. target encoding), and why feature scaling matters for some algorithms but not others —
these decisions separate pipeline operators from ML practitioners. Hands-On ML Chapter 2 covers these
techniques comprehensively (ML in Production) .
The first exposure to OpenAI’s API marks the transition toward AI engineering. Understanding how
to structure prompts, handle API responses, and manage rate limits is foundational for all subsequent

LLM work. Start with simple completion requests before moving to embeddings — the embeddings API
is what powers RAG systems, which you’ll build in Week 8.

Week 6 introduces deep learning with PyTorch — and this is where framework choice matters.
Research consistently shows PyTorch is the better choice for beginners in 2025: it’s more Pythonic, has

cleaner debugging (standard Python debuggers work), and dominates the research community which
means better tutorials and pre-trained models (acecloud.ai) . TensorFlow’s Keras API is simpler for
basic models, but PyTorch’s flexibility pays dividends when you move to custom architectures.
For
ML internships, PyTorch knowledge is increasingly expected — especially for roles involving LLMs or
computer vision.

computer vision.
Understanding neural networks at the implementation level (not just calling model.fit()) is crucial.
Building MNIST from scratch with PyTorch — defining the nn.Module, implementing the training loop
with autograd, and manually computing loss — gives you the intuition that makes debugging complex
models possible later. The jump from scikit-learn’s declarative API to PyTorch’s imperative style is
significant but necessary for any serious ML work.

significant but necessary for any serious ML work.
Ollama becomes your local LLM infrastructure this week. Setting up Ollama to run models like Llama
3.1 locally gives you unlimited experimentation without API costs (T Recommendation H.263) . The
setup is remarkably simple — one-line installation, then ollama run llama3.1 gets you a ChatGPT-like
interface running entirely on your machine. This enables rapid experimentation with prompt engineering,

model comparison, and eventually RAG pipeline development without worrying about per-token pricing.

Week 7 is where your plan’s AI/LLM focus truly materializes. LangChain has become the standard

Week 7 is where your plan’s AI/LLM focus truly materializes. LangChain has become the standard
framework for building LLM applications, and the latest v0.3 release significantly streamlined the API
(Udemy) .
The core abstractions — ChatModels, PromptTemplates, Chains, and Agents — provide a
consistent interface for combining LLMs with external data sources and tools. Understanding when to

consistent interface for combining LLMs with external data sources and tools. Understanding when to
use a simple Chain versus a full Agent with tool-calling capabilities is a key architectural decision in LLM
application design.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is the most important LLM pattern for practical appli-
cations. Instead of relying on an LLM’s static training knowledge, RAG retrieves relevant documents

cations. Instead of relying on an LLM’s static training knowledge, RAG retrieves relevant documents
from a vector database and injects them into the prompt context — dramatically improving accuracy
for domain-specific queries (wordpress.com) . Building a complete RAG pipeline involves: (1) document
loading and chunking, (2) embedding generation (using OpenAI or local models via Ollama), (3) vec-
tor storage in ChromaDB, (4) similarity search for relevant chunks, and (5) response generation with

retrieved context. This is a substantial project that becomes a major portfolio piece.
ChromaDB is the recommended vector database for beginners — it’s lightweight, open-source, and has
excellent LangChain integration (Agix Technologies) . For prototyping and learning, it requires zero
infrastructure setup (runs embedded in your Python process). Understanding vector similarity search —
how embeddings convert text into high-dimensional vectors and how cosine similarity finds “close” vectors

— is foundational modern AI engineering knowledge.

Week 8 integrates everything into production-like projects. The AI Email Triage Bot combines multi-
ple skills: using LangChain to process emails, vector storage for historical context, LLM summarization,

and a Streamlit dashboard for user interaction. This isn’t a toy project — it’s architecturally similar
to real enterprise AI tools. Building it demonstrates that you can combine APIs, databases, and UI
components into a cohesive application.
LangGraph (LangChain’s extension for building agent workflows) enables multi-step reasoning where
an agent can plan, execute tools, observe results, and iterate — the “agent loop” pattern that powers

sophisticated AI applications (onlinetutorials.me) . Understanding this pattern is increasingly important
as companies move beyond simple Q&A chatbots to AI systems that can actually perform tasks.
Deployment skills — building Flask APIs, containerizing with Docker, and hosting on platforms like
Render or Hugging Face Spaces — transform notebooks into production artifacts. An ML model that
only runs on your laptop is a prototype; an ML model accessible via REST API is a product.

Week 9 is project sprint week. The goal is completing two substantial portfolio projects:
Project 1: AI Knowledge Base Assistant — A full RAG application that ingests documents (PDFs,
Markdown files, or web pages), stores them in a vector database, and answers questions via a Streamlit
interface. This demonstrates LangChain, vector databases, embeddings, and UI development. Deploy it

interface. This demonstrates LangChain, vector databases, embeddings, and UI development. Deploy it
on Streamlit Community Cloud for a live demo link you can share with recruiters.
Project 2: Data-Driven Recommendation Engine — Use clustering (K-Means or DBSCAN) on a
purchase history dataset to segment users, then build a simple content-based recommender using scikit-
learn. Expose recommendations via a Flask API with proper documentation. This demonstrates classical

ML skills alongside API development — showing versatility across the ML stack.
The key to portfolio projects is README quality. Each project needs: (1) clear problem statement,
(2) tech stack list, (3) setup instructions, (4) architecture diagram, (5) demo screenshots or GIFs, and (6)
discussion of challenges faced and trade-offs made. A project with a great README gets attention; a
project with code-only gets ignored.

10. Final Recommendations & Success Factors
The single most important success factor for this plan is consistency over intensity. Forty hours per

week is substantial but sustainable if you maintain daily DSA practice (1.5-2 hours) and block larger
chunks for project work. Missing a day of DSA practice creates a compounding deficit — the pattern
recognition that makes you fast at problem-solving requires repeated exposure. Conversely, the ML/AI
content is more forgiving of scheduling variations because projects can absorb focused weekend sessions.
Start applying before you feel “ready”. The job market rewards momentum — early applications

Start applying before you feel “ready”. The job market rewards momentum — early applications
generate interview practice (which reveals gaps you can fill), feedback on your resume, and potentially
early offers that reduce pressure. Begin submitting applications in Week 8, even as you’re still building
projects. Many companies have multi-week interview processes, so applications submitted in Week 8
might lead to interviews in Week 10 when your projects are polished.

Finally, document your learning publicly. Write short LinkedIn posts about what you’re building,

even as a beginner, builds relationships that lead to referrals and insider opportunities.
